PowerShell: Microsoft's command-line shell and scripting language, which passes objects between commands.
Why the command line

A graphical user interface (GUI) is fine for one machine. The command line is faster and works over Secure Shell (SSH). It can be scripted across hundreds of machines. Most security tools are command-line first.
Linux essentials

`ls -la` lists files, including hidden ones. `cd` moves around, `cat` prints a file, `less` pages through it and `grep` finds matching lines. `ip a` shows addresses and `ss -tulpn` shows listening ports.
Windows essentials
`ipconfig /all` shows network settings. `ping` and `tracert` test whether you can reach a host. `nslookup` queries the Domain Name System (DNS), and `netstat -ano` lists connections with process IDs.
Pipes

A pipe, the | symbol, sends one command's output into the next. `journalctl -u ssh | grep "Failed password" | wc -l` counts failed SSH logins. Chaining small tools is how most quick investigations work.
PowerShell objects

PowerShell passes objects, not plain text, between commands. So you can filter by a property, such as a service's status: `Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq Running`. That makes it powerful for admins, and for attackers too.
Getting help

Most tools have built-in help that lists their flags, meaning command options. On Linux, use `man grep` or `grep --help`. In PowerShell, use `Get-Help Get-Process -Examples`. Reading help quickly is a real skill.
real: Help desk: “the internet's down”

A user can't reach anything. If `ipconfig` shows 169.254.x.x, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) failed, so check the cable, Wi-Fi and DHCP server. If the address looks normal, ping the gateway, then a public IP, then try nslookup. In two minutes you know if it's the link, DHCP, routing or DNS.
myth: You have to memorise every command and flag.
Professionals look things up all the time. Know the core tools well, and look up the rest.

tryit.p: Kali logs to the systemd journal, so read SSH logs with journalctl. Start SSH, fail a login on purpose, then count the failures and see which IP they came from. Stop SSH afterwards.
tryit.code:
sudo systemctl start ssh
ssh nobody@127.0.0.1    # type yes, any password, then Ctrl+C
sudo journalctl -u ssh | grep -c "Failed password"
sudo journalctl -u ssh | grep "Failed password" |
  awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c
sudo systemctl stop ssh

quiz.q: Which Linux command lists listening ports and the processes using them?
quiz.w: ss -tulpn. It shows sockets: -t for Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), -u for User Datagram Protocol (UDP), -l listening, -p process, -n numeric. Use sudo to see other users' processes. Not ls -la: it lists files. Not cd /ports: cd only changes folder.

quiz.q: `ipconfig` shows the address 169.254.10.7. What's the most likely problem?
quiz.w: No DHCP server answered. 169.254.x.x is a self-assigned address, called Automatic Private IP Addressing (APIPA). Windows uses it when no DHCP server replies. Not DNS or a blocked site: neither changes the PC's own address.

quiz.q: In `ps aux | grep sshd`, what does the `|` do?
o: Sends the output of ps into grep
Saves the output to a file called grep
quiz.w: It sends the output of ps into grep. A pipe feeds one command's output to the next command's input. Not saving to a file: `>` does that. Not running them separately: the pipe links them.

quiz.q: Which Windows command lists connections with their process IDs?
quiz.w: netstat -ano. -a shows all connections, -n keeps addresses numeric and -o adds the process ID (PID). Not ipconfig /all: it shows network settings. Not tracert: it traces the route to a host.

recap: Linux: ls, cd, cat, grep, ip a, ss -tulpn, journalctl.
Windows: ipconfig, ping, tracert, nslookup, netstat -ano.
Pipes chain small tools into an investigation.
Use man, --help and Get-Help instead of memorising.

days.sub: Two-way locks and one-way fingerprints.
learn: Key terms

Symmetric encryption: encryption that uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt.
Asymmetric cryptography: cryptography that uses a key pair, made of a public key and a private key.
Hash: a short fingerprint of data that changes if the data changes.
Digital signature: a cryptographic mark that proves who signed data and that it wasn't altered.
Encryption

Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the right key can read it. It protects data at rest (stored) and in transit. Don't confuse it with encoding, like Base64, which anyone can reverse without a key.
Symmetric: one shared key

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. The standard algorithm is the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). It's fast enough for disks and virtual private network (VPN) traffic. The hard part is sharing the key safely.
Asymmetric: a key pair

Asymmetric cryptography uses a key pair. What the public key encrypts, only the private key can decrypt. RSA (named after its inventors Rivest, Shamir and Adleman) and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) are common. It's slow, so it's mainly used to agree keys and to sign things.
Hashing

A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length digest, like the 256 bits of Secure Hash Algorithm 256 (SHA-256). It's one-way: you can't reverse it. But short or common inputs can be guessed and checked. Change one character and the digest changes completely.
Digital signatures

To sign, you hash a message and sign the hash with your private key. Anyone with your public key can check it. That proves integrity and who signed. Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates and software updates rely on this.
Storing passwords

Hash passwords with a slow, salted algorithm like bcrypt or Argon2. The salt, a random value per password, makes identical passwords produce different hashes. The slowness makes cracking expensive. Fast hashes like MD5 (Message Digest 5) are the wrong tool.
real: Adobe, 2013

In 2013 attackers stole data on around 150 million Adobe accounts. The passwords were encrypted instead of hashed, using Triple Data Encryption Standard (3DES). All used the same key and mode, so identical passwords looked identical. Plain-text password hints sat right next to them, which made many easy to guess.
myth: A matching hash proves who published a file.
A hash proves the file wasn't changed, as long as you trust where the hash came from. Only a digital signature proves who published it.

tryit.p: Hash two words that differ by one letter and compare the digests. Then hash a file you've downloaded and compare it with the value the publisher lists.
tryit.code:
import hashlib
for word in ["hello", "hellp"]:
    print(word, hashlib.sha256(word.encode()).hexdigest())

# File hash, Linux:   sha256sum kali.iso
# File hash, Windows: Get-FileHash .\kali.iso

quiz.q: You check a downloaded ISO disk image's SHA-256 against the publisher's. What does that confirm?
quiz.w: Integrity. A matching hash shows the file wasn't altered or corrupted. Not confidentiality: a hash doesn't hide the contents. Not availability: it doesn't keep the download working or reachable.

quiz.q: A message is encrypted with Alice's public key. Which key decrypts it?
quiz.w: Alice's private key. Only the matching private key can decrypt, which is why the public key can be shared freely. Not Alice's public key: anyone can have it, so it can't unlock the message. Not the sender's private key: it isn't part of Alice's key pair.

quiz.q: Which of these is a symmetric encryption algorithm?
quiz.w: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard). It uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. Not RSA: it's asymmetric, using a key pair. Not SHA-256: it's a hash, not encryption.

quiz.q: Two users have the same password, but their stored hashes are different. Why?
o: Each was hashed with a unique salt
Each was encrypted with its own key
quiz.w: Each was hashed with a unique salt. The same input always gives the same hash, so the salt changes the input. That also stops precomputed tables working. Not random output: that's the trap, as hashing isn't random. Not separate keys: hashing uses no key.

recap: Encryption is reversible with a key: confidentiality.
Symmetric (AES) is fast; asymmetric (RSA, ECC) agrees keys and signs.
Hashing is one-way: integrity.
Passwords: bcrypt or Argon2 with a salt, never plain encryption.

days.sub: Break things safely, and keep the mess in the lab.
learn: Key terms

Hypervisor: software that runs virtual machines.
Virtual machine (VM): a computer simulated in software, running inside a real one.
Snapshot: a saved state of a VM that you can roll back to.
VM escape: code in a VM breaking out to reach the host machine.
Hypervisors

A hypervisor runs virtual machines (VMs), each with its own operating system (OS). Type 1 runs directly on the hardware, called bare metal: Proxmox, ESXi, Hyper-V. Type 2 runs on top of an OS: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.
Why labs use VMs
VMs let you build, break and rebuild systems for free. A snapshot saves a known-good state, so you can roll back in seconds after an exercise. The cloud is built on the same idea.
VirtualBox: modes that reach out
In network address translation (NAT) mode, the VM reaches the internet through the host. NAT Network mode also lets VMs see each other. In bridged mode, the VM joins your real home network.
VirtualBox: lab-only modes
In internal mode, VMs talk only to each other. In host-only mode, VMs talk to each other and to the host.
Isolation isn't guaranteed
VMs reduce risk, but they don't guarantee isolation. Shared folders, a shared clipboard, drag and drop, bridged networking and hypervisor bugs can all leak. Turn off what you don't need.
Lab rules
Keep vulnerable VMs on an internal or host-only network, never bridged. Snapshot before each exercise. Keep the hypervisor patched. Keep real passwords and personal files out of lab VMs.
real: VENOM, 2015

In 2015 researchers disclosed VENOM, a bug in the virtual floppy controller used by the QEMU emulator, Xen, Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) and VirtualBox. Code in a VM could potentially break out to the host. Few people had thought about the floppy drive. Every device a hypervisor emulates is attack surface, another possible way in.
myth: NAT mode keeps a vulnerable VM safely hidden.
A VM in NAT mode can still reach the internet and your home network. Use internal or host-only.

tryit.p: Put each VM on the internal network labnet, turn off clipboard and drag and drop, then snapshot it (VirtualBox 7 syntax). Remove shared folders under Settings, Shared Folders.
tryit.code:
VBoxManage modifyvm "Win-Target" --nic1 intnet --intnet1 "labnet"
VBoxManage modifyvm "Win-Target" --clipboard-mode disabled --drag-and-drop disabled
VBoxManage snapshot "Win-Target" take "clean-baseline"
# Repeat for your Kali VM, so both share labnet

quiz.q: Which network mode should a deliberately vulnerable VM use?
quiz.w: Internal or host-only. Both keep the VM inside the lab. Not bridged: it puts the VM on your real home network. Not whatever the default is: check the mode yourself, because some modes reach the internet.

quiz.q: Which of these is a Type 2 hypervisor?
quiz.w: VirtualBox. It runs as an app on top of your OS. Not ESXi or Proxmox: both are Type 1, running directly on the hardware.

quiz.q: Why take a snapshot before a lab exercise?
o: To roll back if it breaks
quiz.w: To roll back if it breaks. If the exercise breaks or infects the VM, you restore the known-good snapshot in seconds. Not encryption or network isolation: a snapshot only saves the VM's state.

quiz.q: Your lab VMs are on an internal network, but a shared folder maps your host's Documents folder. What's the risk?
o: The VM will lose its IP address
Code in the VM could reach your files
quiz.w: Code in the VM could reach your files, to read or change them. The network is only one path out; shared folders, clipboard and drag and drop are others. Not none: that's the trap, as internal mode only covers the network. Not a lost IP: folders don't affect addressing.

recap: Type 1 runs on hardware; Type 2 runs on an OS.
Bridged joins your real network; internal and host-only don't.
VMs reduce risk but don't guarantee isolation.
Vulnerable VMs go on internal or host-only networks, never bridged.

days.sub: Operating systems and crypto, pulled together.
learn: Key terms

Hashing rounds: the number of times a password is hashed, which makes each guess slower.
Least privilege: giving each person and process only the access their job needs, for only as long as they need it.
Hardening: changing insecure default settings to shrink the attack surface.
How to review
Try to answer each review card's heading from memory before you read the body. Then do the hands-on task. You remember what you do far better than what you reread.
real: LastPass, 2022

In 2022 attackers stole backups of LastPass customer vaults, where users keep saved passwords. Each vault was encrypted with a key derived from the user's master password. So safety depended on password strength and hashing rounds. Some old accounts had very low settings, and saved website addresses weren't encrypted.
myth: chmod 777 is a safe fix for permission errors.
It lets everyone read, write and run the file. Grant only what's needed, such as 640 or 750.

tryit.p: Create a test user, make a file in /tmp only you can read, and confirm the test user gets “Permission denied”. Then clean up. A mail spool warning from userdel is harmless.
tryit.code:
sudo useradd -m tester
echo "top secret" > /tmp/private.txt
chmod 600 /tmp/private.txt
sudo -u tester cat /tmp/private.txt
rm /tmp/private.txt
sudo userdel -r tester

review: Linux vs Windows
Linux: text config under /etc, logs under /var/log or the journal, packages via apt or dnf. Windows: the Registry, Event Viewer, Active Directory and Group Policy.
Permissions
rwxr-x--- is 750: owner everything, group read and execute, others nothing. chmod changes it, chown changes the owner, sudo elevates one command. Watch for root-owned set user ID (SUID) programs.
Processes and services
A process is a running program with a process ID (PID), a user and a parent. A service runs in the background, often on a port. Suspicious: wrong path, odd parent, unknown listener.
Command line
Linux: ls -la, grep, ss -tulpn, journalctl, systemctl. Windows: ipconfig /all, netstat -ano, Get-Process, Get-Service. Pipes chain them together.
Crypto in one card

Symmetric, such as Advanced Encryption Standard (AES): one key, fast. Asymmetric, such as RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman) or elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC): key pair, for key agreement and signatures. Hashing, such as Secure Hash Algorithm 256 (SHA-256): one-way, for integrity. Passwords: bcrypt or Argon2 with a salt.
Lab safety
Internal or host-only networks for vulnerable virtual machines (VMs), never bridged. Snapshot before exercises. Turn off shared folders and clipboard. Keep the hypervisor patched.

quiz.q: What's the right way to store user passwords?
o: Encrypted with a strong AES key
quiz.w: Hashed with bcrypt or Argon2. These slow, salted algorithms make cracking expensive. Not AES encryption: if the key leaks, every password is exposed. Not MD5 (Message Digest 5): it's far too fast, so guessing is cheap.

quiz.q: What's the octal value of rw-r--r--?
quiz.w: 644. rw- is 6, r-- is 4 and r-- is 4, so everyone may read but only the owner may change it. Not 600: that's rw-------, owner only. Not 755: that's rwxr-xr-x.

quiz.q: HTTPS uses asymmetric cryptography in the handshake, then symmetric encryption for the data. Why?
o: Asymmetric is too slow for bulk data
quiz.w: Asymmetric is too slow for bulk data. So it authenticates and agrees a shared key, then fast symmetric ciphers such as AES encrypt the traffic. Not less secure: symmetric encryption is strong. Not key expiry: speed is the reason.

quiz.q: Where are most traditional Linux log files kept?
quiz.w: /var/log. It holds text logs. Many newer systems also use the systemd journal, read with journalctl. Not /etc: it holds configuration. Not /home: it holds users' files.

quiz.q: An unknown service on a Windows server listens on port 4444 and runs from C:\ProgramData\upd.exe. What's your best first step?
quiz.w: Record the details and escalate it as a possible compromise. Note the path, hash, parent and connections, then follow your incident process. Not deleting: it destroys evidence and may not remove the attacker. Not ignoring: a service nobody installed is a warning sign.

quiz.q: Where would you look for a program that starts every time a user logs on to Windows?
o: The Run keys in the Registry
quiz.w: The Run keys in the Registry. Run keys for the machine (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE) and the user (HKEY_CURRENT_USER) are classic persistence spots, along with scheduled tasks and services. Not /etc/shadow: it's a Linux password file. Not the firewall log: it records traffic.

quiz.q: Which VirtualBox mode lets VMs talk to each other and the host, with no internet access?
quiz.w: Host-only. It's a private network shared with the host; internal is the same without the host. Not network address translation (NAT): it reaches the internet through the host. Not bridged: it joins your real network.

quiz.q: What proves a software update really came from its publisher?
quiz.w: A valid digital signature. It ties the file to the publisher's private key. Not HTTPS: it only protects the download from whichever server you used. Not file size: an altered file can have the same size.

recap: Know where config, logs and services live on both systems.
Read permissions in rwx and octal.
Symmetric, asymmetric and hashing each have one job.
Lab VMs stay off bridged networks.

days.sub: See your network the way an attacker would.
learn: Key terms

Reconnaissance: gathering information about a target before an attack.
Host discovery: finding which addresses on a network belong to live devices.
SYN scan: a port scan that starts the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) handshake but never finishes it, also called a half-open scan.
Intrusion detection system (IDS): a tool that watches network or system activity and alerts on signs of an attack.
What Nmap does

Nmap is a network scanner. It finds live hosts, open ports, running services and their versions. Defenders use it to check their own exposure, and attackers use it for reconnaissance (gathering information before an attack). Same tool, different permission.
Permission first
Only scan systems you own or have written permission to test. Unauthorised scanning can breach laws and acceptable use policies. It also sets off alarms. Your internal lab is the place to practise.
Host discovery

`sudo nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24` finds live hosts without scanning ports. As root on a local subnet, Nmap uses Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) requests, so even hosts that block ping show up. Without sudo, it falls back to weaker probes.
The SYN scan

`sudo nmap -sS` sends a SYN (synchronise) packet to each port. That's the first step of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) handshake. The reply shows the port's state. SYN-ACK means open, RST (reset) means closed, and no reply or an error message means filtered.
Why it's called half-open
After a SYN-ACK, Nmap doesn't send the final ACK (acknowledgement). So Nmap never completes the handshake. That's why a SYN scan is called a half-open scan.
Versions, OS and scripts
`-sV` identifies the service and version on open ports. `-O` guesses the operating system (OS). `-sC` runs default scripts for extra detail.
Which ports get scanned
By default, Nmap scans the 1,000 most common TCP ports. `-p-` scans all 65,535. User Datagram Protocol (UDP) services, such as Domain Name System (DNS), need `-sU`.
From results to risk
A port list is an inventory. Compare each service and version with what should be there. Then look up known vulnerabilities for those versions. Open isn't the same as vulnerable.
real: The internet is always scanning

Services such as Shodan and Censys scan the whole IPv4 internet continuously and index what they find. Anything you expose can be listed within days, such as Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) or an old admin page. Attackers often search these indexes instead of scanning themselves.
myth: A SYN scan is stealthy, so nobody notices it.
Skipping the final ACK avoids some application logs. But firewalls and intrusion detection systems (IDS) spot a burst of SYNs easily. You'll see that for yourself in the Day 25 lab.

tryit.where: Kali, against the Windows target only
tryit.p: Find live hosts, scan the top ports, then identify versions. With the Windows firewall on, expect mostly filtered ports.

quiz.q: Why is `-sS` called a half-open scan?
o: It scans only half of the ports
It probes only half of the hosts
quiz.w: It doesn't finish the handshake. After the SYN-ACK, Nmap doesn't send the final ACK, so a full connection is never made. Not half the ports or hosts: the name describes the connection, not how much gets scanned.

quiz.q: What does `nmap -sn` do?
quiz.w: Finds live hosts only. -sn is host discovery, a quick, quiet first step with no port scan. Not all ports: that's -p-. Not versions: that's -sV.

quiz.q: Which flag tells Nmap to identify service versions?
quiz.w: -sV. It probes open ports to work out the service and version, which you need before looking up vulnerabilities. Not -sS: it finds open ports. Not -sn: it finds live hosts only.

quiz.q: When is it OK to scan a network?
o: If you only run a stealthy SYN scan
If you own it or have written permission
If the host is reachable from the internet
quiz.w: If you own it or have written permission. Permission is what separates a security test from an attack, so get it in writing. Not a SYN scan: the scan type doesn't make it allowed. Not internet hosts: being reachable isn't permission.

recap: Only scan what you own or have written permission to test.
-sn finds hosts, -sS finds ports, -sV finds versions.
Open, closed and filtered come from SYN-ACK, RST or silence.
A scan result is an inventory, not a list of vulnerabilities.

days.sub: What's really on the wire.
learn: Key terms

Capture filter: a filter that decides which packets Wireshark records.
Display filter: a filter that decides which recorded packets Wireshark shows you.
Metadata: data about traffic, such as addresses, ports and timing, rather than its content.
Session cookie: a token a website stores in your browser to keep you logged in.
What Wireshark does

Wireshark captures packets from a network interface. It decodes every layer, from Ethernet up to Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). It shows what's really on the wire, not what an app claims is happening.
Capture vs display filters

Capture filters decide what gets recorded. They use Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax, such as `host 10.10.10.20`. Display filters decide what you see afterwards, such as `ip.addr == 10.10.10.20`. You can change display filters at any time.
Display filters to know
Learn these display filters by heart. `dns`, `http`, `tls`, `arp` and `icmp` each show one protocol. `tcp.port == 443` shows traffic on port 443.
Spot new connections

`tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0` shows new connection attempts. It matches packets with SYN (synchronise) set and ACK (acknowledgement) clear. Combine filters with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not).
Follow the stream

Right-click a packet and choose Follow, then TCP Stream. This rebuilds a whole conversation on one Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection. With cleartext protocols you can read requests, responses and even passwords. With Transport Layer Security (TLS) you see only encrypted data.
What TLS still reveals

Even encrypted traffic shows IP addresses, ports, timing and how much data moved. The TLS handshake usually shows the server name too. This data about the traffic is called metadata. It's often enough to spot something odd.
Capture responsibly
Only capture on networks you own or are authorised to monitor. Packets can hold passwords and personal information. So store capture files carefully, and delete them when you're done.
real: Firesheep, 2010

Session cookies keep you logged in. In 2010 a Firefox add-on called Firesheep let anyone on public Wi-Fi grab other people's session cookies with one click. It worked on sites such as Facebook and Twitter. They used HTTPS for the login page, but not for the rest of the session. The outcry pushed big sites to use HTTPS everywhere.
myth: Wireshark sees all traffic on the network.
On a switched network you mostly see your own traffic and broadcasts. Seeing other hosts needs a mirror port or a network tap.

tryit.p: Start Wireshark on Kali with sudo and capture on eth0. Serve a folder over plain HTTP on port 8080, which Wireshark decodes as HTTP. Browse to it from Windows. Then follow the TCP stream and read the request.
tryit.code:
# Kali: serve the current folder over plain HTTP
python3 -m http.server 8080

# Windows browser
http://10.10.10.10:8080

# Wireshark display filter on Kali
http && ip.addr == 10.10.10.20

quiz.q: Which of these is Wireshark display filter syntax?
quiz.w: ip.addr == 10.10.10.20. A field name with == is display filter syntax. Not the other three: they're capture filters, written in Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax.

quiz.q: Which display filter shows new TCP connection attempts?
quiz.w: The filter with ack == 0. A new connection starts with SYN set and ACK clear. Not ack == 1: that shows SYN-ACK replies. Not the FIN (finish) filter: it shows connections closing. Not udp: User Datagram Protocol (UDP) has no handshake.

quiz.q: You capture HTTPS traffic to a website. What can you usually still see?
quiz.w: The traffic metadata: IP addresses, ports, timing and usually the server name. That's often enough for an investigation. Not the page contents or password: TLS encrypts both.

quiz.q: What does Follow TCP Stream do?
quiz.w: Rebuilds one conversation. It stitches the packets of one connection back together, in order, so you can read the exchange. Not blocking: Wireshark only watches traffic. Not decrypting: TLS content stays encrypted without the session keys.

recap: Capture filters decide what's recorded; display filters decide what you see.
Know dns, http, tls, arp and the SYN-without-ACK filter.
Follow TCP Stream rebuilds a conversation.
TLS hides content but not metadata.

days.sub: The record of what really happened.
learn: Key terms

Event ID: a number that identifies the type of event in a Windows log, such as 4625 for a failed logon.
Logon type: a number in a Windows logon event that shows how someone logged on, such as 10 for Remote Desktop.
Security information and event management (SIEM): a system that collects logs from many systems in one place, correlates them and raises alerts.
Network Level Authentication (NLA): a Remote Desktop setting that makes users log in before a full remote session starts.
Why logs matter

Logs record logins, errors, changes and connections. Without them you can't detect an attack or prove what an attacker did. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10:2025 lists Security Logging and Alerting Failures as A09.
Linux logs

Where Linux records logins depends on the distribution. Systems running rsyslog, such as Ubuntu, write authentication events to /var/log/auth.log. The Red Hat family uses /var/log/secure. By default, newer Debian and Kali log only to the systemd journal, where `journalctl -u ssh` shows Secure Shell (SSH) events.
Windows Security log

Event Viewer's Security log records logons and account changes. Learn these Event IDs by heart. 4624: successful logon. 4625: failed logon. 4672: special (admin-level) privileges at logon. 4720: user account created. 1102: audit log cleared.
Logon types
Events 4624 and 4625 include a logon type, which shows how someone tried to log on. Type 2 is at the keyboard. Type 3 is over the network, such as a file share. Type 10 is Remote Desktop.
Failed RDP can show as type 3
With NLA on, failed Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) logons often show as type 3. So check the source IP too.
SIEMs

A security information and event management (SIEM) system collects logs from many systems in one place. It correlates them and raises alerts. Wazuh is a free, open-source option; Microsoft Sentinel and Splunk are common at work. Alerts only help if someone acts on them.
Red flags

Red flags include many failures then a success from the same IP. Others are a 3am logon from a new country, a new admin account or a cleared Security log. Any one might be innocent. Together, they can reveal an attack.
real: Target's ignored alerts, 2013

Remember Target from Day 9? Its malware detection tool raised alerts as the attackers set up. A monitoring team overseas passed them on, but the team in the US didn't act on them in time. Logging and alerting only help when someone responds.
myth: No alerts means no attacks.
Silence might mean you aren't collecting the right logs, or nobody has tuned the alerts. Attackers clear logs too, which is why Event ID 1102 matters.

tryit.p: Lock the Windows target and enter a wrong password three times. Then log in and list the failed logons. If nothing shows, check that logon auditing is turned on.
tryit.code:
# Windows PowerShell (admin)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625} -MaxEvents 5 |
  Format-List TimeCreated, Message

auditpol /get /subcategory:"Logon"

quiz.q: Hundreds of Event ID 4625 entries arrive from one IP in a minute. What do they suggest?
quiz.w: A password-guessing attack, such as brute force or password spraying. 4625 is a failed logon, and a burst from one source is a classic sign. Not a backup or update: they don't fail hundreds of logons a minute.

quiz.q: Event ID 1102 appears on a server at 2am. Why worry?
o: It logs a routine nightly backup
quiz.w: Someone cleared the Security log, possibly to hide what they did. That's rare in normal operations and common after an intrusion, so investigate who did it. Not a password change or backup: neither creates Event ID 1102.

quiz.q: Many 4625 events with logon type 10 arrive from one external IP. What's being targeted?
quiz.w: Remote Desktop. Type 10 is RemoteInteractive, which is Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). Not a file share: that's usually type 3, though failed RDP logons with NLA on can show as type 3 too. Not the keyboard: that's type 2.

quiz.q: What does OWASP Top 10:2025 call A09?
quiz.w: Security Logging and Alerting Failures. The 2025 list renamed A09 to stress alerting. Not Security Logging and Monitoring Failures: that was the 2021 name. Not Insufficient Logging: it isn't the 2025 name.

recap: Linux: auth.log, secure or journalctl.
Logon type 3 is network and 10 is RDP. With NLA, failed RDP often shows as 3.
A SIEM centralises logs, but someone has to act on alerts.

days.sub: Attack your own lab and see what the defender sees.
learn: Key terms

Port scan: probing many ports on a host to see which ones answer.
Firewall log: a file where a firewall records the traffic it allowed or blocked.
Security operations centre (SOC): a team that monitors an organisation's systems and responds to alerts.
The plan
You'll scan the Windows target from Kali. At the same time, you'll watch with Wireshark and the Windows firewall log. Seeing both sides of one attack is the fastest way to learn detection.
Set up

Put both virtual machines (VMs) on the labnet internal network: Kali at 10.10.10.10 and Windows at 10.10.10.20. Snapshot both first. Confirm they can see each other with `sudo nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24`.
Turn on firewall logging
Windows Defender Firewall doesn't log dropped packets by default. Turn logging on (see the Try it card). The log is saved at C:\Windows\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log.
Run the scan

Start Wireshark on Kali's eth0. Apply the display filter `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0`. Then run the SYN (synchronise) scan. You'll see a burst of SYNs from one source hit many ports in seconds.
Compare the evidence

In Wireshark, Statistics then Conversations shows one source talking to many ports. On Windows, the firewall log shows a DROP line for each blocked probe. What did the scan learn, and what did the defender see?
real: A scan from the inside

Security operations centre (SOC) analysts treat scans very differently depending on where they come from. Scans from the internet are constant background noise. An internal laptop scanning the server subnet often means a compromised machine looking for its next target.
myth: If a scan didn't show up in Event Viewer, nothing recorded it.

A SYN scan rarely creates logon events. Firewall logs, network flow records (summaries of who talked to whom) and intrusion detection systems all see it. Detection depends on looking in the right place.

tryit.p: Turn on firewall logging and watch the log on Windows. Then scan from Kali and watch the DROP lines arrive. Afterwards, restore both clean snapshots.
tryit.code:
# Windows PowerShell (admin)
Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -LogBlocked True
Get-Content C:\Windows\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log -Tail 20 -Wait

# Kali
sudo nmap -sS --top-ports 200 10.10.10.20

# Windows: turn logging off again
Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -LogBlocked False

quiz.q: What pattern in Wireshark shows a port scan?
o: A SYN burst across many ports
quiz.w: A SYN burst across many ports. A scanner probes many ports fast, so you see SYNs from one IP to many destination ports. Not one encrypted session or Domain Name System replies: both are normal traffic.

quiz.q: Once logging is on, where does Windows Defender Firewall record dropped packets?
o: The Security log as Event ID 4625
quiz.w: pfirewall.log. The firewall writes its own text log. Not /var/log/auth.log: that's a Linux log. Not Event ID 4625: that's a failed logon in the Security log.

quiz.q: Most ports on the Windows target show as filtered. What does that tell you?
o: The Windows VM is switched off
quiz.w: The firewall is dropping probes. Filtered means no useful reply came back. Not open: an open port answers the probe. Not switched off: Nmap would show a powered-off host as down, not filtered.

quiz.q: A finance laptop starts scanning the server subnet at midnight. What's the most likely explanation?
quiz.w: A possible compromise. Workstations rarely scan servers in normal operations. Treat it as possible lateral movement, an attacker moving sideways from one system to another inside a network. Not a backup or update: neither probes a whole subnet.

recap: Snapshot first, internal network only.
Turn on firewall logging to see the drops.
Wireshark shows a burst of SYNs from one source.
An internal machine scanning servers is a red flag.

days.sub: Layers before, a plan during, lessons after.
learn: Key terms

Incident response: the plan and steps for detecting, containing and recovering from a security incident.
Containment: stopping an incident from spreading, such as by isolating a machine from the network.
US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0: a framework that sorts security work into six functions, like Govern.
Blameless review: a review after an incident that looks for what failed, not who to blame.
Defence in depth

Defence in depth means stacking controls so one failure doesn't become a breach. Layers include training, multi-factor authentication (MFA), patching, firewalls, segmentation, endpoint protection, logging and backups. Each layer is another chance to stop or spot an attacker.
Types of control

Good defence mixes three types of control. Preventive controls stop things, such as MFA and firewalls. Detective controls spot them, such as logs and alerts. Corrective controls fix things afterwards, such as backups and reimaging (rebuilding from a clean image).
The four-phase cycle

Special Publication (SP) 800-61 is a US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) guide to incident response. Revision 2 (Rev. 2) described four phases. They are preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. You'll still see them in textbooks and interviews.
Rev. 3 and CSF 2.0

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) instead organises incident response around the six Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 functions. They are Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Preparation is now spread across Govern, Identify and Protect.
Contain first
Isolate the machine from the network first, but don't switch it off, because memory holds evidence. Preserve logs, note what you do and when, and escalate.
Then remove and recover
Once the incident is contained, remove its cause. Then recover from clean backups.
Learn from it
After recovery, hold a blameless review and fix the gaps. A blameless review looks for what failed, not who to blame.
Report serious breaches

If personal information was breached and serious harm is likely, report it. In Australia, report it to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC). In New Zealand, report it to the Privacy Commissioner.
real: Maersk and NotPetya, 2017

In June 2017 NotPetya malware spread through shipping giant Maersk, wiping thousands of machines within hours. Every domain controller, the servers that hold Active Directory, was hit except one. That one, in Ghana, happened to be offline during a power cut. That one copy let Maersk rebuild its network in about ten days.
myth: Incident response starts when you get breached.
Most incident response work happens before an incident. It means knowing your assets and having backups, logging, contacts and a written plan ready.

tryit.where: Notes app or your GitHub repo
tryit.p: Write a one-page playbook (a step-by-step response plan) for “a user entered their password on a phishing page”. Cover who to tell, resetting the password and signing out all sessions. Then add which logs to check and what to tell the user.

quiz.q: What does NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 align incident response with?
quiz.w: The CSF 2.0 functions. Rev. 3 is built on CSF 2.0, so incident response sits under its six functions. Not the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model: it describes network layers. Not the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10: it lists web app risks.

quiz.q: A laptop shows signs of ransomware. What should you do first?
o: Run a disk clean-up to remove it
Switch it off at the wall straight away
Isolate it from the network, leave it on
quiz.w: Isolate it from the network and leave it on. Isolating stops the spread, and keeping it on preserves memory evidence such as running processes and keys. Not switching off: you lose that evidence. Not a clean-up: it won't stop the spread.

quiz.q: Which of these is a detective control?
quiz.w: Alerts on failed logons. Alerts detect an attack. Not multi-factor authentication: it's a preventive control. Not restoring from backup: it's a corrective control.

quiz.q: What are the six CSF 2.0 functions?
o: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Prepare, Detect, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Review
quiz.w: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. CSF 2.0 added Govern to the five functions of CSF 1.1. Not the five-item list: that's CSF 1.1. Not the list starting with Prepare: those aren't the CSF function names.

recap: Defence in depth: many layers, no single point of failure.
Preventive, detective and corrective controls.
Rev. 2 had four phases; Rev. 3 uses the CSF 2.0 functions.
Isolate, preserve evidence, escalate, recover, then review and report.

days.sub: Four weeks, one last pass.
learn: Key terms

Third-party access: access to your systems or data held by an outside company, such as a vendor.
Data retention: how long an organisation keeps data before deleting it.
How to review
Answer each review card's heading out loud before you read the body. Then do the quiz without scrolling back. Anything you miss tells you which day to redo.
real: Latitude Financial, 2023

In March 2023 attackers got a Latitude Financial employee's login through an attack on a major vendor. They took about 14 million Australian and New Zealand records. These included millions of driver licence numbers, some kept since 2005. Latitude refused to pay. One breach shows two risks: third-party access and long data retention.
myth: Once you've finished Levels B1 to B4, the basics are done.
Most breaches exploit the basics, such as missing multi-factor authentication (MFA), unpatched systems, weak access control and ignored alerts. You'll use these ideas at every level.

tryit.p: From memory, write down the key ports, Windows Event IDs, MFA ranking, permission octals and the six Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 functions. Then check your sheet against the cards. Keep it for interview prep.

review: Level B1

Confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA): double extortion hits all three. Threats include insiders and accidents. Risk combines likelihood and impact. Authorisation is checked on every request, with least privilege. SMS (text message) codes count as MFA but are weak. Only FIDO2 keys and passkeys are phishing-resistant.
Level B2

An open port means a service is listening, not that it's vulnerable. Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) has a handshake; User Datagram Protocol (UDP) doesn't. A laptop reaches a website using Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), Domain Name System (DNS), TCP and Transport Layer Security (TLS). The padlock means encrypted, not honest.
Level B3

Linux config lives in /etc, and Windows config in the Registry. Read permissions in rwx and octal. Judge a process by its path and parent, not its name. Hash passwords with bcrypt or Argon2. Vulnerable virtual machines (VMs) never go on bridged networks.
Level B4

Nmap finds hosts, ports and versions, with permission only. Wireshark shows what's on the wire. Logs and a security information and event management (SIEM) system catch what attackers leave behind. Incident response now follows the CSF 2.0 functions. Defence in depth means no single control does everything.
Explain: SMS MFA

SMS codes count as MFA, but SIM swapping and fake login pages can steal them. Authenticator app codes can be phished too. FIDO2 keys and passkeys check the real domain, so a phishing site gets nothing.
Explain: open ports

Open just means a service is listening. Risk depends on what it is, its version, its configuration and who can reach it. Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) open to the internet is risky. Port 443 on a patched web server is expected.
Explain: backups
Offline or immutable backups restore encrypted data and get you running again. They do nothing about data that's already been stolen, the other half of double extortion.
Explain: HTTPS

Transport Layer Security (TLS) checks the server's certificate, agrees session keys, then encrypts traffic between browser and server. The data is decrypted at the server, so stored data needs its own protection.

quiz.q: Which of these statements is true?
o: Passkeys resist phishing better than SMS
Backups stop attackers stealing your data
An open port proves there's a vulnerability
quiz.w: Passkeys resist phishing better than SMS. A passkey only works on the real site it was created for. Not backups: they restore data but can't undo theft. Not open ports: open means listening, not vulnerable.

quiz.q: In the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10:2025, what is A09?
quiz.w: Security Logging and Alerting Failures. That's the 2025 name for A09. Not the Monitoring version: that was the 2021 name. Not Broken Access Control: it's A01. Not Injection: it's A05.

quiz.q: Ransomware steals data, then encrypts it. Which pillars of the CIA triad does it hit?
quiz.w: All three pillars. Theft breaks confidentiality, unauthorised encryption breaks integrity and lost access breaks availability. Not any single pillar: double extortion hits all three at once.

quiz.q: Which of these is the most worrying open port?
o: 443 open on a patched web server
Unpatched RDP open to the internet
53 open on the internal DNS server
quiz.w: Unpatched RDP open to the internet. Exposed, unpatched Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is a common ransomware entry point. Not 443 or 53: both are expected services, patched or internal.

quiz.q: Which document set out the four-phase incident response cycle?
quiz.w: NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP 800-61 Rev. 2. It set out the four phases. Not Rev. 3 (April 2025): it organises incident response around the CSF 2.0 functions. Not the OWASP Top 10: it lists web app risks.

quiz.q: Which network mode should a deliberately vulnerable VM use?
o: NAT with port forwarding to the internet
quiz.w: Internal or host-only. Both keep vulnerable machines off your real network and away from the internet. Not bridged: it joins your real network. Not network address translation (NAT) with port forwarding: it exposes the VM to the internet.

quiz.q: A file owned by alice, group staff, is set to 640. What can a staff member who isn't alice do?
quiz.w: Read it. In 640, 6 gives the owner rw-, 4 gives the group r-- and 0 gives others nothing. Not read and write: only alice has that. Not nothing: that applies to users outside the group.

quiz.q: What does hardening mean?
o: Adding a bigger firewall in front
quiz.w: Changing insecure defaults, which shrinks the attack surface. Hardening removes or changes default credentials, unneeded services, open ports and unused software. Not keeping vendor defaults: they're often insecure. Not a bigger firewall: hardening changes the system itself.

recap: You can explain CIA, risk, access control and MFA strength.
You can trace a connection from DHCP to TLS.
You can read permissions, processes, hashes and logs.
Score 80% or more on every day before Level B5.

days.sub: From fundamentals to a job-ready portfolio.
learn: Key terms

Portfolio: a collection of your own work, such as lab write-ups, that shows employers your skills.
Certification: an exam-based qualification, such as CompTIA Security+.
Deliberately vulnerable virtual machine (VM): a VM built with known flaws so you can practise attacks safely.
What you've covered
You've covered security fundamentals, networking, operating systems, cryptography, scanning, packet capture and logs. That's the base every intermediate topic builds on.
Add a vulnerable target
Add a deliberately vulnerable virtual machine (VM), such as Metasploitable 2. Keep it on the internal network only.
Add a SIEM
Add a security information and event management (SIEM) system, such as Wazuh, and send it Windows and Linux logs. Give Wazuh 4 to 8 GB of RAM. Then attack your lab and detect yourself.
Show your work
Write up each lab on GitHub: goal, setup, steps, what you saw and what you'd fix. Screenshots and clear explanations beat a list of courses.
Keep write-ups safe
Never publish real credentials or anything from an employer's systems. Keep write-ups to your own lab.
First certification
CompTIA Security+ is a common first security certification. It often appears in entry-level job ads. Pair any certification with lab write-ups.
Cloud certifications
For cloud roles, start with an entry-level certification, such as AWS Cloud Practitioner or Microsoft SC-900. Then aim for a cloud security certification.
Next: B5, then intermediate

Next is Level B5 (Microsoft and cloud identity). After that, the intermediate stage goes deeper into security frameworks. These include the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, ISO 27001 and the Essential Eight. It also covers security tools, configuring controls, vulnerability management and cloud security basics.
Keep the habit

A few cards a day beats a cram. Redo any day marked red in the Days picker. Follow alerts from the Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) and New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). Read one incident write-up a week.
real: What hiring managers look for

Entry-level security roles usually want networking and operating system basics, log analysis, some scripting and clear communication. IT support experience is a real asset. You already troubleshoot, document and calm down stressed users. Say that in interviews, with examples.
myth: Certifications alone will get you hired.
Certifications help you get past hiring filters. But interviews test whether you can do and explain the work, and documented lab projects prove that.

tryit.p: Create a public repository (repo) called homelab. Add a README for your Day 25 lab, using this outline. Keep it short, and use screenshots from your own lab only.
tryit.code:
# Lab 01: Scan and watch
## Goal
Detect an Nmap SYN scan from the defender's side.
## Setup
VirtualBox internal network. Kali 10.10.10.10, Windows 10.10.10.20.
## Steps
## What I saw
## What I'd change in a real network

quiz.q: What's the strongest evidence of skill for an employer?
quiz.w: Documented lab projects. Write-ups of real lab work show what you can do, not just what you've read. Not videos watched: they show study, not skill. Not memorised ports: useful, but they don't prove you can do the work.

quiz.q: Where should Metasploitable 2 be connected in your lab?
o: NAT with ports forwarded from the internet
quiz.w: An internal or host-only network. Metasploitable 2 is deliberately full of holes, so it must never be reachable from your home network or the internet. Not bridged: it joins your home network. Not network address translation (NAT) with forwarded ports: it exposes the VM.

quiz.q: Which of these must stay out of a public lab write-up?
o: What you'd do differently next time
quiz.w: Real logins or employer details. Publishing real credentials or work details is a breach in its own right. Not screenshots from your own lab or what you'd change: both belong in a good write-up.

quiz.q: What does a security information and event management (SIEM) system add to your lab?
quiz.w: Central logs and alerting. A SIEM lets you practise the defender's job: collecting logs, writing detections and responding to alerts. Not faster internet: it doesn't change your network. Not a target: that's Metasploitable 2's role.

recap: Levels B1 to B4 done: fundamentals, networking, OS, crypto, hands-on analysis.
Grow the lab with a vulnerable VM and a SIEM, kept internal.
Write up everything on GitHub, but never real credentials or work data.
Next: Level B5 (Microsoft and cloud identity), then the intermediate stage.

days.sub: The identity system behind Microsoft 365 and Azure.
learn: Key terms

Microsoft Entra ID: Microsoft's cloud identity service for Microsoft 365 and Azure, called Azure Active Directory until 2023.
Tenant: an organisation's own private instance of Entra ID, holding its users, groups and apps.
Privileged Identity Management (PIM): an Entra ID feature that lets people switch on an admin role only when they need it.
Service principal: an app's identity in Entra ID, which lets it sign in and hold permissions.
What Entra ID is

Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service. It was called Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) until 2023. It holds the users, groups, devices and apps for Microsoft 365 and Azure. It also handles their sign-ins.
On-premises AD

On-premises Active Directory (AD) runs on an organisation's own servers. It uses Kerberos, NT LAN Manager (NTLM) and Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It also has organisational units (OUs) and Group Policy.
Not AD in the cloud

Entra ID uses web protocols, not the Kerberos and LDAP of on-premises Active Directory (AD). Examples are OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML). Many organisations run both and sync accounts with Microsoft Entra Connect.
Admin roles

Admin rights in Entra ID come from roles. Global Administrator can change almost anything, so Microsoft recommends fewer than five of them. Narrower roles cover most day-to-day work, such as User Administrator, Helpdesk Administrator and Security Reader.
Just-in-time admin

With Privileged Identity Management (PIM), few people hold standing admin rights that an attacker could steal. Instead, people switch on an admin role only when they need it, for a few hours. Activation uses multi-factor authentication (MFA) and, optionally, approval. PIM needs Entra ID P2 or Entra ID Governance licences.
Apps are identities too

Enterprise applications and service principals sign in and get permissions, just like people. An app with broad access to mail or files is as valuable to an attacker as an admin account. So review app permissions as well as people's.
real: Midnight Blizzard, 2024

In January 2024 Microsoft disclosed an attack by a Russian state group. The group password-sprayed a legacy test tenant account that had no multi-factor authentication (MFA). It then abused an old test OAuth app with elevated access. Through it, the group reached email belonging to senior leaders and security staff.
myth: Entra ID is just Active Directory in the cloud.

Many skills transfer, but Entra ID is a separate system with its own attacks. One is consent phishing, which tricks users into giving a malicious app access. Another is token theft, which steals proof that a user has already signed in.

tryit.p: Use Microsoft Graph PowerShell in a tenant you own, such as a free trial. It lists the roles switched on in your tenant, then who holds one right now. People only eligible through Privileged Identity Management (PIM) won't appear.
tryit.code:
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "RoleManagement.Read.Directory"
Get-MgDirectoryRole | Select-Object DisplayName, Id
Get-MgDirectoryRoleMember -DirectoryRoleId <role-id>

quiz.q: What was Microsoft Entra ID called before 2023?
quiz.w: Azure Active Directory. Microsoft renamed Azure AD to Entra ID in 2023, but the service itself didn't change. Not Active Directory Domain Services: that's on-premises AD. Not Microsoft Intune: it manages devices.

quiz.q: How many Global Administrators does Microsoft recommend?
quiz.w: Fewer than five. Global Administrator can change almost anything, so keep it to a few people. Not one per department or at least ten: more holders means more accounts for attackers to target.

quiz.q: What does Privileged Identity Management (PIM) add?
o: Admin roles used only when needed
A second copy of every user account
quiz.w: Admin roles used only when needed. This just-in-time access means far fewer standing admin rights wait to be stolen. Not a second copy of accounts: PIM doesn't duplicate users. Not encryption: PIM controls who holds admin roles.

quiz.q: How did the attackers first get into Microsoft in the 2024 Midnight Blizzard incident?
quiz.w: Password spraying a test account. A forgotten legacy test account had no multi-factor authentication (MFA). Old accounts need the same controls as new ones. Not a zero-day (a flaw attackers use before a fix exists) or a stolen laptop: neither was the way in.

recap: Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure AD.
It uses OAuth, OpenID Connect and SAML, not Kerberos and LDAP.
Keep Global Administrators under five; use PIM for just-in-time admin.
Apps and service principals need permission reviews too.

days.sub: If-then rules that check every sign-in.
learn: Key terms

Conditional Access: Entra ID rules that block a sign-in, allow it or require more, such as multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Security defaults: a free, simpler Entra ID setting that makes everyone register for MFA and blocks legacy authentication.
Legacy authentication: old sign-in protocols, such as basic authentication for email, that can't do MFA.
Emergency access (break-glass) account: an admin account for getting back in if everyone else is locked out.
If-then rules for sign-ins

Conditional Access policies are if-then rules for sign-ins. A policy checks the user, app, location, device or risk. Then it blocks the sign-in, allows it or requires something extra. That could be multi-factor authentication (MFA) or a compliant device, one that meets your organisation's device rules.
When it runs
Conditional Access is checked after the first sign-in step. At that point, Entra ID knows who is signing in.
Licences and security defaults

Conditional Access needs Entra ID P1 licences, and risk-based conditions need Entra ID P2. Organisations without P1 can turn on security defaults instead. These require multi-factor authentication (MFA) in a simpler, all-or-nothing way.
Test before you enforce
Every new policy can run in report-only mode first. Sign-in logs then show what would have happened. That way, you catch a policy that would lock out a whole team before it does.
Block legacy authentication

Block legacy authentication, because it can't do multi-factor authentication (MFA). Legacy authentication means old protocols, such as basic authentication for email. Password spraying, which tries one common password on many accounts, targets them for this reason. A policy that blocks them closes the gap.
Emergency access accounts

Emergency access accounts save you if a bad policy locks everyone else out. Keep at least two cloud-only break-glass accounts, excluded from your Conditional Access policies. Protect them with phishing-resistant MFA, such as FIDO2 keys kept somewhere safe. Alert on every use.
real: One setting, huge effect

In 2019 Microsoft reported that multi-factor authentication (MFA) could block over 99.9% of account compromise attacks. Most organisations use Conditional Access to require MFA in the right places. They also use it to block the legacy protocols that can't use MFA.
myth: Conditional Access replaces MFA.
Conditional Access works with multi-factor authentication (MFA), not instead of it. Without MFA or a phishing-resistant method behind a policy, there's nothing strong for it to require.

tryit.p: In your own test tenant, open Conditional Access. It's under Entra ID or Protection, depending on your portal version. Create a policy that requires MFA for a test user, and set it to report-only. Sign in as that user, then check the Conditional Access details in the sign-in log. Exclude your emergency account from every policy.

quiz.q: What's the best way to test a new Conditional Access policy?
o: Test it on the Global Administrator first
Use report-only, then check the sign-in logs
Turn it on for everyone, then watch for issues
quiz.w: Use report-only, then check the sign-in logs. Report-only mode shows what would happen without blocking anyone. Not everyone at once: a bad policy could lock out a whole team. Not the Global Administrator: a mistake could lock out your top admin.

quiz.q: Why block legacy authentication?
quiz.w: It can't do MFA. Legacy protocols never ask for multi-factor authentication (MFA), so password sprays target them. Not speed or licence cost: the risk is attackers getting around MFA.

quiz.q: What are emergency access (break-glass) accounts for?
o: Getting back in after a lockout
quiz.w: Getting back in after a lockout, such as from a bad policy or an outage. They skip Conditional Access but keep phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) and monitoring. Not everyday work or sharing: any use should be rare and alert someone.

quiz.q: A small business has no Entra ID P1 licences. What's the simplest way to require multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
o: Write a Conditional Access policy anyway
quiz.w: Turn on security defaults. They give free, baseline MFA for everyone. Not a Conditional Access policy: it needs P1 licences. Not opt-in: staff who skip it stay unprotected.

recap: Conditional Access is if-then rules for sign-ins.
It needs P1; security defaults are the free baseline.
Test in report-only, block legacy authentication.
Keep at least two monitored break-glass accounts outside the policies.

days.sub: Two permission systems, often confused.
learn: Key terms

Azure role-based access control (RBAC): the permission system for Azure resources, such as virtual machines and storage.
Scope: the level a role applies at, from a management group down to a single resource.
Security principal: a user, group or app that can be given a role.
Role assignment: a link between a security principal, a role definition and a scope.
Two permission systems

Microsoft has two separate permission systems. Entra roles control the directory: users, groups, apps and organisation-wide settings. Azure role-based access control (RBAC) controls Azure resources, such as virtual machines, storage and networks. Power in one doesn't automatically give you power in the other.
Scopes flow down

Azure RBAC roles are assigned at a scope. From widest to narrowest, scopes are management group, subscription, resource group and single resource. Assignments flow down. So Owner on a subscription means Owner on everything inside it.
Owner, Contributor, Reader

Three common built-in roles are Owner, Contributor and Reader. Owner can manage everything, including granting access. Contributor can create and change resources but can't grant access. Reader can only look.
Resources, not data
Owner, Contributor and Reader manage resources, not the data inside them. Reading blobs, the files kept in Azure Blob Storage, needs a data role. One example is Storage Blob Data Reader.
Three-part assignments

A role assignment links three things: a security principal, a role definition and a scope. A security principal is a user, group or app. Assign roles to groups, not individuals, at the narrowest scope that works.
real: Owner to save time

Cloud reviews often find a contractor with Owner on a whole subscription, given “to save time”. That contractor could grant access to anyone and delete anything. Contributor on one resource group would have done the job.
myth: Global Administrator automatically controls every Azure subscription.
Not by default. But a Global Administrator can elevate themselves to User Access Administrator over all subscriptions. That switch is logged, and it should trigger an alert.

tryit.p: List every role assignment for a user across all scopes. Then read what a built-in role allows. Look for Owner where Contributor or Reader would do.
tryit.code:
az login
az role assignment list --assignee user@example.com --all --output table
az role definition list --name Contributor --output json

quiz.q: Which permission system controls who can manage Azure virtual machines?
quiz.w: Azure RBAC. Azure role-based access control (RBAC) controls Azure resources, such as virtual machines. Not Entra roles: they control the directory. Not Group Policy: it pushes settings from on-premises Active Directory.

quiz.q: What can Owner do that Contributor can't?
quiz.w: Grant other people access. Owner manages both resources and access. Not creating virtual machines or reading storage accounts: Contributor can do both, because it manages resources.

quiz.q: Someone is Reader on a subscription. What can they do in a resource group inside it?
quiz.w: View its resources. Assignments at a higher scope flow down to everything below. Not nothing: scopes do inherit. Not change: Reader can only look.

quiz.q: A contractor needs to manage the resources in one app's resource group. What's the best assignment?
quiz.w: Contributor on that resource group. It's the narrowest role at the narrowest scope that works. Not Owner on the subscription: it can grant access and reaches everything. Not Global Administrator: it controls the directory, not Azure resources by default.

recap: Entra roles run the directory; Azure RBAC runs resources.
Scopes run from management group to resource, and inherit down.
Owner grants access; Contributor can't; Reader only reads.
Assign to groups at the narrowest scope.

days.sub: What endpoint detection sees, and how you respond.
learn: Key terms

Endpoint detection and response (EDR): a tool that records what happens on devices, so you can detect, investigate and respond to attacks.
Device isolation: cutting a device off from the network while it stays connected to Defender.
Advanced hunting: a Defender tool for searching up to 30 days of security data, such as device and email events, with queries.
Kusto Query Language (KQL): Microsoft's query language for searching log data, used in Defender and Sentinel.
More than antivirus

Antivirus blocks known bad files. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) records what processes, files, network connections and logons do. That lets you spot suspicious behaviour and investigate it. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is a common example.
Attack surface reduction rules
Defender for Endpoint's attack surface reduction rules stop common attack steps outright. One example blocks Office apps from creating child processes, which are programs started by another program.
Alerts become incidents

Defender groups related alerts into incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal. One incident might combine a phishing email, a malicious document and a PowerShell download. These can span several devices.
The device timeline

Each device has a timeline and a process tree, which shows which program started which. Together they let you follow exactly what happened. For example, Word started PowerShell, which connected to an IP address and downloaded a file.
Response actions

From the Defender portal, you can isolate a device from the network, run an antivirus scan, collect an investigation package or use live response. Live response gives you a remote shell on the device. Isolation keeps the device connected to Defender, so you can keep investigating.
Advanced hunting

Advanced hunting answers the question “has this happened anywhere else?” It runs Kusto Query Language (KQL) queries over 30 days of data. Tables include DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents and DeviceLogonEvents.
real: A typical alert

A security operations centre (SOC) analyst gets a “Suspicious PowerShell command line” alert on a finance laptop. The process tree shows Word as the parent. The analyst isolates the device, then uses advanced hunting to look for the same command on other devices. They find one more, and both are contained within minutes.
myth: EDR is just antivirus with a new name.
Endpoint detection and response (EDR) can catch new techniques that antivirus has never seen. It also lets you investigate what happened and respond across many devices.

tryit.p: In a Defender trial or lab, run this query. It finds devices and accounts with many failed logons in the last day.
tryit.code:
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| summarize failures = count() by DeviceName, AccountName
| top 10 by failures

quiz.q: What does endpoint detection and response (EDR) add to antivirus?
o: A firewall for the whole network
quiz.w: A record of device behaviour. EDR gives you visibility and response, not just blocking known files. Not a network firewall: EDR works on each device. Not faster downloads: it doesn't change network speed.

quiz.q: Why isolate a device instead of switching it off?
o: It's faster to switch back on later
Switching off would delete the malware
It keeps evidence and the Defender link
quiz.w: It keeps evidence and the Defender link. An isolated device can't spread anything, but you can still investigate it, and memory evidence survives. Not deleting malware: switching off loses memory evidence instead. Not speed: the reason is evidence.

quiz.q: Which table records process launches in advanced hunting?
quiz.w: DeviceProcessEvents. It holds process creation, including command lines and parent processes. Not DeviceLogonEvents: it records logons. Not SigninLogs: it holds Entra ID sign-ins, not device activity.

quiz.q: You find one device running a malicious command. What's the best next question?
o: Has it run on any other device?
When was the device last patched?
quiz.w: Has it run on any other device? Scope comes next, and advanced hunting across all devices shows how far it has spread. Not patching or who installed Defender: those can wait until you know the scope.

recap: EDR records behaviour; antivirus blocks known files.
Alerts are grouped into incidents in the Defender portal.
Isolate devices to contain them without losing evidence.
Advanced hunting uses KQL across Device tables.

days.sub: From log to alert to closed incident.
learn: Key terms

Security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR): tools that automate response steps, such as disabling a user.
Analytics rule: a Sentinel query, usually run on a schedule, that looks for suspicious patterns and raises alerts.
Entity: something an alert involves, such as an account, host or IP address.
Alert fatigue: when so many alerts arrive that analysts start to miss real ones.
What Sentinel is

Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud security information and event management (SIEM) system. It's also a security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) tool. It's built on a Log Analytics workspace.
Moving to the Defender portal
Sentinel is moving fully into the Microsoft Defender portal. Sentinel in the Azure portal is due to retire on 31 March 2027.
How alerts are made

Data connectors bring in logs from Entra ID, Defender, firewalls and more. Analytics rules look for suspicious patterns and raise alerts. They're usually scheduled Kusto Query Language (KQL) queries. Sentinel then groups the alerts into incidents.
Entities
Entities make linking related activity much faster. Alerts map entities, such as accounts, hosts and IP addresses. Click an entity to see everything Sentinel knows about it.
Working an incident
Assign the incident to yourself and set it to Active. Check the severity, then investigate the entities and evidence. Write good notes, because they help the next analyst.
Closing an incident

Close each incident with a classification: true positive, benign positive, false positive or undetermined. A benign positive is real, detected activity that wasn't malicious, such as approved admin work. The Defender portal words these classifications slightly differently.
Automation

Automate the repetitive steps, and keep people for judgement. Automation rules can assign, tag or close incidents. Playbooks are automated workflows built on Azure Logic Apps. They can take actions such as disabling a user or posting to Teams.
real: Tuning the noise

A new security operations centre (SOC) turns on dozens of analytics rules. It gets hundreds of incidents a day, most of them benign. Analysts start skimming. Tuning the noisiest rules with exclusions and thresholds lets the real incidents stand out.
myth: More analytics rules always means better detection.
Fewer, well-tuned rules beat many noisy ones. Untuned rules cause alert fatigue, and real attacks get lost in the noise.

tryit.p: Open Microsoft's free Log Analytics demo environment, which may ask you to sign in. Try this summary query. If the table is empty or missing, pick another from the list on the left and adapt the query.
tryit.code:
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| summarize events = count() by EventID
| top 10 by events

quiz.q: In Sentinel, what turns a Kusto Query Language (KQL) query into alerts?
quiz.w: An analytics rule. It runs a query to detect suspicious patterns and raise alerts. Not a data connector: it brings data in. Not a workbook: it visualises data.

quiz.q: An incident turns out to be a real admin doing approved work. How should it be closed?
quiz.w: Benign positive. The detection was right and the activity happened, but it wasn't malicious. Not true positive: that means real malicious activity. Not false positive: that means the detection was wrong.

quiz.q: What are Sentinel playbooks built on?
quiz.w: Azure Logic Apps. Playbooks are Logic Apps workflows that take response actions, automatically or on demand. Not Python scripts on a server or Excel macros: Sentinel playbooks don't run on either.

quiz.q: Analysts are ignoring incidents because most are noise. What's the best fix?
quiz.w: Tune the noisiest analytics rules. Alert fatigue is a tuning problem, and fewer, better alerts get real attention. Not more rules: they add noise. Not closing low-severity incidents unread: real attacks can hide among them.

recap: Sentinel is a cloud SIEM and SOAR on Log Analytics.
Connectors bring data; analytics rules raise alerts; incidents group them.
Close each incident with a classification, such as benign positive.
Tune rules to beat alert fatigue.

days.sub: Which of ten thousand findings do you fix first?
learn: Key terms

Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE): an ID that names one publicly known vulnerability.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS): a 0 to 10 score for how severe a vulnerability is.
Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS): an estimate of how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited in the next 30 days.
Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue: a US government list of flaws that attackers are exploiting in the wild.
CVE IDs name flaws

A Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) ID names one publicly known vulnerability. An example is CVE-2021-44228. Scanners match the software and versions you run against CVEs. They often return thousands of findings.
CVSS: how severe

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) rates severity from 0 to 10. Under CVSS v3, 9.0 and above is critical, 7.0 to 8.9 high, 4.0 to 6.9 medium, 0.1 to 3.9 low and 0.0 none. CVSS v4.0 came out in 2023.
EPSS: how likely

The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) estimates the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days. It comes from FIRST, the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams. A medium CVSS flaw with a high EPSS can matter more than a critical one nobody exploits.
KEV: already happening

The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue lists flaws attackers are using in the wild. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) runs it. If something you run is on it, it goes to the top of the list. That's especially true if it's internet-facing.
Putting it together
Fix internet-facing systems with known or likely exploitation first. A KEV listing is one sign of known exploitation. A high EPSS score is one sign of likely exploitation.
Essential Eight patch times

From Maturity Level One, the Essential Eight asks for online services to be patched within 48 hours in two cases. One is when the vendor rates a flaw critical. The other is when a working exploit exists. Otherwise, patch within two weeks.
real: Citrix Bleed, 2023

CVE-2023-4966 in Citrix NetScaler leaked session tokens, which prove a user is logged in. Attackers exploited it as a zero-day (a flaw attackers use before a fix exists) from late August 2023, before the October patch. Patching stopped new leaks, but stolen sessions kept working. So Citrix told customers to kill all active sessions too. Ransomware groups used it against large organisations.
myth: Always patch the highest CVSS score first.
A high CVSS score shows severity, not likelihood. Exposure, exploitation in the wild (KEV) and probability of exploitation (EPSS) often matter more than the raw score.

tryit.p: Get a CVE's exploitation probability from FIRST's free EPSS service. Then count the entries in CISA's KEV catalogue.
tryit.code:
curl -s "https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss?cve=CVE-2023-4966"

curl -s https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json |
  python3 -c "import json,sys; print(len(json.load(sys.stdin)['vulnerabilities']), 'known exploited')"

quiz.q: What does the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) estimate?
o: How long a vendor takes to patch it
Its chance of exploitation in 30 days
quiz.w: Its chance of exploitation in the next 30 days. Not severity: that's the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Not patch time: EPSS doesn't measure vendors. Use CVSS and EPSS together.

quiz.q: A flaw in your internet-facing virtual private network (VPN) is in the KEV catalogue. What does that tell you?
o: It mainly matters to US agencies
quiz.w: Attackers are exploiting it now. The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue lists flaws used in the wild, so internet-facing plus KEV goes to the top. Not low priority: it's the opposite. Not just US agencies: anyone running that software is at risk.

quiz.q: Under CVSS v3, what rating does a score of 9.8 get?
quiz.w: Critical. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3, 9.0 to 10.0 is critical. Not high: that's 7.0 to 8.9. Not medium: that's 4.0 to 6.9.

quiz.q: Why wasn't patching enough for Citrix Bleed?
quiz.w: Stolen sessions kept working. A patch closes the hole, but session tokens already stolen stay valid until you kill the sessions. Not a missing patch: one came out in October. Not new flaws: the patch worked. Revoke sessions, tokens and credentials too.

recap: CVE names the flaw; CVSS rates severity.
EPSS estimates likelihood; KEV confirms exploitation.
Internet-facing plus exploited goes first.
After patching, revoke what may have been stolen.

days.sub: Microsoft and cloud identity, pulled together.
learn: Key terms

Foothold: an attacker's first point of access inside a system or network.
Perimeter: the boundary where you control who and what gets in.
How to review
Answer each review heading out loud before you read it. Then do the quiz without scrolling back. These topics come up often in junior security operations centre (SOC) and cloud interviews.
real: Putting the week together

A Sentinel alert shows a sign-in to a contractor account from a new country, without multi-factor authentication (MFA). Conditional Access should have required MFA. The account had Owner on a subscription. Defender shows a new process on a server. Every topic this week touches that one incident.
myth: Cloud security is a completely different field from what you've learned.

The ideas are the same: identity, least privilege, logging, detection and patching. The names and tools change, such as Entra roles, Azure role-based access control (RBAC), Conditional Access, Sentinel and Defender.

tryit.p: Use the real-world card's scenario. In half a page, write what you'd check first and which logs you'd query. Then write what you'd contain and which control would have stopped it. Use it as an interview answer and a portfolio piece.

review: Entra ID

Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). It uses web protocols, not Kerberos. Keep Global Administrators under five. Use Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for just-in-time admin, and review app permissions too.
Conditional Access

Conditional Access policies are if-then sign-in rules. They block, allow, or require MFA or a compliant device. They need Entra ID P1; otherwise, use security defaults. Test in report-only mode, block legacy authentication and keep break-glass accounts.
Azure RBAC versus Entra roles
Entra roles run the directory. Azure RBAC runs resources, at scopes that inherit downwards. Owner grants access, Contributor can't, and Reader only reads.
Defender and Sentinel
Defender for Endpoint records device behaviour and lets you isolate devices and hunt. Sentinel collects logs, raises alerts from analytics rules and groups them into incidents.
Vulnerability management

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) measures severity. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) measures likelihood. The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue confirms exploitation. Fix internet-facing, exploited flaws first, and revoke stolen sessions after patching.

quiz.q: Which Microsoft feature can require multi-factor authentication (MFA) only for risky or external sign-ins?
quiz.w: Conditional Access. It checks conditions like location and risk before deciding what to require, and risk needs Entra ID P2. Not Azure role-based access control (RBAC): it controls Azure resources. Not Defender for Endpoint: it protects devices.

quiz.q: A user can create virtual machines (VMs) but can't give anyone else access. Which Azure role fits?
quiz.w: Contributor. It manages resources without managing access. Not Owner: it can also grant access. Not Global Administrator: it's an Entra role for the directory, not an Azure role.

quiz.q: Which Sentinel component turns a scheduled Kusto Query Language (KQL) query into alerts?
quiz.w: Analytics rule. It runs a scheduled query and raises alerts. Not a data connector: it brings data in. Not a workbook: it visualises data.

quiz.q: What's the best way to contain a compromised laptop in Defender for Endpoint?
o: Switch it off at the wall
quiz.w: Isolate the device. Isolation cuts it off from the network but keeps the evidence and the Defender connection. Not switching off: memory evidence is lost. Not uninstalling Defender: you lose your view of the device.

quiz.q: Two flaws: CVSS 9.1 with no known exploitation on an internal server, and CVSS 7.5 in KEV on your internet-facing virtual private network (VPN). Which first?
quiz.w: The VPN flaw in KEV. Exposure and active exploitation beat raw severity. Being in Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) means attackers use it now. Not the 9.1 flaw: the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) measures severity, not likelihood. Not age: it doesn't show risk.

quiz.q: Why keep emergency access accounts outside Conditional Access?
o: So they can skip MFA without anyone noticing
So a broken policy can't lock every admin out
Because Conditional Access can't apply to admins
quiz.w: So a broken policy can't lock every admin out. They're your way back in. Not skipping MFA unnoticed: protect them with phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) and alert on every use. Not admin limits: Conditional Access can apply to admins.

quiz.q: What did Midnight Blizzard abuse after its first foothold at Microsoft in 2024?
quiz.w: An old test OAuth app. It had elevated access, which let the attackers reach senior leaders' email. Unused apps with broad permissions are a quiet route to sensitive data. Not a firewall or USB drive: neither was involved.

recap: Identity is the cloud perimeter: Entra ID, Conditional Access, PIM.
Least privilege in Azure: narrow roles at narrow scopes.
Detect with Sentinel, respond with Defender.
Patch by exposure and exploitation, not just score.
